title: Project Foundation
text:
1. Career Pathway


Selected career pathway: Data Analytics
Why we selected it: Data Analytics was selected because it represents a broad and practical career pathway that appears across many technology-driven organizations. It also allows the team to evaluate multiple related role types while focusing on the skills, qualifications, compensation, and market conditions most relevant to aspiring analytics professionals.

title: Project Foundation
text:
2. Industry Selection


Selected industry: Computer Systems Design and Related Services NAICS code: 5415

Industry Justification
Computer Systems Design and Related Services is highly relevant to the Data Analytics career pathway because organizations in this industry rely heavily on data, software, information systems, and technology-enabled decision-making. The course dataset also provides a substantially larger analytical sample for this industry, supporting more meaningful analysis of labor-market patterns.


Role of Analytics in This Industry
Analytics professionals in this industry support areas such as business intelligence, data analysis, systems performance, technology consulting, reporting, forecasting, and data-driven decision-making. These roles may require candidates to interpret large datasets, identify trends, build reports and dashboards, and translate analytical findings into recommendations for clients or internal business teams.

title: Project Foundation
text:
3. Target User



User Profile
The target user is a student, recent graduate, or early-career professional interested in pursuing an analytics-related career within the Computer Systems Design and Related Services industry. The user may have foundational experience with data analysis, statistics, business analytics, or related disciplines and some exposure to tools such as Excel, SQL, Python, R, or data visualization platforms. However, they may have limited professional experience in technology-focused organizations and may not yet understand how their existing skills align with available analytics roles.


User Needs
Before applying for analytics positions in Computer Systems Design and Related Services, the target user needs a clearer understanding of the types of analytics roles available, the technical and professional skills employers commonly request, typical education requirements, salary expectations, geographic and remote work patterns, and potential skill gaps. This information can help the user evaluate their current qualifications and identify which skills or experiences they should prioritize to become a more competitive candidate.

title: Project Foundation
text:
4. Product Question



Primary Question

How can an aspiring analytics professional evaluate career opportunities in Computer Systems Design and Related Services and determine which skills, qualifications, and experiences to prioritize to become a competitive candidate?



Supporting Questions

What analytics roles appear most frequently in Computer Systems Design and Related Services?
Which technical and professional skills are most commonly requested?
How do salary, experience, location, and remote-work patterns vary?
Where does the target user have skill gaps?
Which skills should the target user prioritize?

title: Project Foundation
text:
5. Project Rationale



Problem Statement
Students and early-career professionals may not have a clear understanding of the skills and job-market needs required for analytics roles within Computer Systems Design and Related Services, which can result in difficulty identifying appropriate roles and determining how well their qualifications align with employer expectations.


Why the Question Matters
Understanding these requirements is important because students and early-career professionals may need more than general analytics knowledge when preparing for a career in a specific industry. Knowing which skills, qualifications, and experience employers are seeking can help job seekers make more informed decisions about their career preparation and identify areas they may need to develop before applying. It also enables them to better communicate their own skill sets to align with market needs.


Value of the Product
The finished product will provide job seekers with the insights and information needed to better position themselves in the job market, assess their skills and identify areas for self-improvement, and better communicate their strengths based on what employers are seeking. By bringing together information about available roles, required skills and qualifications, salary, location, and work arrangements, the product can support users in their job search and help them better understand current market needs.

title: Project Foundation
text:
6. Literature Review

Source 1: NAICS 5415 Industry Definition
Citation: U.S. Census Bureau. (2022). 2022 NAICS definition: Computer Systems Design and Related Services (5415).
Summary and relevance: The U.S. Census Bureau defines NAICS 5415 as establishments that provide computer systems design and related services. This includes work involving computer hardware, software, and communication technologies (U.S. Census Bureau 2022). The definition helps keep our analysis focused on the industry selected by the team.


Source 2: Data Scientist Career Profile
Citation: O*NET OnLine. (2026). Data Scientists, 15-2051.00.
Summary and relevance: O*NET describes Data Scientists as professionals who turn raw data into useful information through programming, visualization, data mining, modeling, and related methods (O*NET OnLine 2026). It also lists tasks such as preparing data, creating charts, explaining results, and recommending data-based solutions. This supports our decision to study several connected analytics roles rather than one exact job title.


Source 3: Skills in Analytics Job Advertisements
Citation: Verma, A., Yurov, K. M., Lane, P. L., & Yurova, Y. V. (2019). An investigation of skill requirements for business and data analytics positions: A content analysis of job advertisements. Journal of Education for Business, 94(4), 243–250.
Summary and relevance: This study compares the skills requested for Business Analyst, Data Analyst, and Data Scientist positions (Verma et al. 2019). It shows that the roles share some skills but also have important differences. This supports the use of job postings to compare related career paths and explains why we grouped several analytics titles while still reporting separate occupation categories.

title: Project Foundation
text:
8. What We Expect to Explore

Within Computer Systems Design and Related Services, we expect analytics opportunities to span several related role types and employer contexts. Our analysis will examine how demand varies across job titles, employers, salary levels, education requirements, geographic markets, and work arrangements. We will also evaluate the skills information available in the dataset while documenting limitations in the source data rather than assuming that missing skills or experience fields represent employer preferences. These expectations will be tested against the data and revised where the evidence supports a different conclusion.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Market Overview
Our cleaned dataset contains 287 job postings related to Data Analytics within NAICS 5415. It includes positions in data analysis, data science, data engineering, business analysis, and business intelligence.
These results describe the postings available in the course dataset. They should not be treated as a complete picture of every analytics job in the United States.

Main Findings

The final dataset contains 287 relevant postings.
Data Scientists and Database Architects are the two largest occupation groups.
Salary information is available for 112 postings.
The median advertised salary midpoint is $150,708.
California has the most postings with an identified state.
Remote and hybrid jobs together account for 41.5% of the dataset.
Some fields have a large amount of missing or unknown information.

title: Market Baseline
section: What This Means for Job Seekers
text:
What This Means for Job Seekers
Job seekers should search across several related titles, including Data Analyst, Data Scientist, Data Engineer, Business Analyst, and Business Intelligence Analyst. Searching only for one title could leave out relevant opportunities.
California has the most postings with a known state, but the data also shows opportunities in Texas, Washington, New York, Virginia, and remote positions.
Candidates may also benefit from showing a mix of technical and business skills. Employers may expect candidates to analyze data, prepare or manage data, explain findings, and connect their work to business needs.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Limitations

The dataset contains 287 selected postings and does not represent the entire U.S. job market.
Salary information is available for only 112 postings.
Experience fields are empty across the source data.
State information is unavailable for 82 postings.
Work arrangement is unknown for 145 postings.
Employer names are not fully standardized.
The skills fields appear to be alphabetically cut off. Skills beginning with letters from D through Z, including Python and SQL, are not available.
The data covers approximately one quarter, so it cannot show annual or seasonal hiring patterns.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Data Source and Connection
The source is the MET CareerCompass 2026 job-postings extract, supplied as 17 Parquet partitions holding 165,386 postings and 115 variables.
The raw files are not committed to this repository. Each team member downloads them from the course-provided folder and points a local path at the download location, as described in the README. The processed panel produced by this page is committed, so the rest of the site renders without access to the raw extract.
Filtering and cleaning run in PySpark through scripts/build_panel.py, which imports two helper modules, scripts/clean_location.py and scripts/clean_salary.py. The script writes one output file, data/processed/career_market_panel.csv.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Industry Filter
We filtered on NAICS_2022_4, the four-digit 2022 NAICS code attached to each posting. The extract also carries two-, three-, five-, and six-digit variants. We used the four-digit field because the assignment specifies four- or six-digit codes, and because NAICS_2022_4_NAME is blank throughout the extract while NAICS_2022_6_NAME is populated and supplies the industry label.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Career-Pathway Filter
Filtering on the word “analyst” alone was not workable. Within NAICS 5415 it returned 621 postings, but the results included security analysts, QA analysts, trade compliance analysts, and IT support analysts. “Analyst” functions as a generic corporate suffix, and including those roles would distort both the skill analysis and the salary distribution.
We therefore defined the role family positively, matching titles that name an analytics role directly rather than excluding unwanted ones after the fact.
Included patterns: data analyst, data scien, business intelligence, bi analyst, data engineer, analytics engineer, business analyst, reporting analyst
Excluded patterns: security, qa, quality assurance, support, trade, exploitation, acceptance testing, network
The exclusion rule removed only two further postings, which confirms the positive definition was doing the work. We kept it in place as a documented check.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Cleaning Decisions

Duplicate Records
All 287 postings carry a unique ID, so the panel contains no exact duplicates. The DUPLICATES field supplied with the extract is blank on every row and provided no help.
Grouping by title, employer, and posted date does surface repeats. Inspection showed these are multi-location postings rather than duplicates: Esri, for example, advertised the same Enterprise Data Engineer role separately for California, Missouri, and Virginia, each with its own record ID. We kept these, since a single opening advertised in three states is three opportunities from a job seeker’s perspective. The effect is that geographic counts are slightly inflated relative to the number of distinct openings, and we note that where geography is discussed.


Salary
Salary required the most cleaning. SALARY_FROM and SALARY_TO are stored as strings and are blank on most rows.
Three rules were applied:

Rows carrying 0.00 were treated as missing rather than as a salary of zero. Four postings had this pattern, all of them cases where the source held a structured MonetaryAmount object the provider could not flatten.
One posting listed an annual salary of $401, which is implausible. We set a floor of $20,000 and excluded it.
Four postings quoted hourly rates. These were converted to annual equivalents at 2,080 hours so that all salary figures sit on one scale.

Skill Fields
The extract carries four skill families. Coverage within the panel is uneven:

SKILLS_NAME: 278 of 287 postings
SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME: 277 of 287
COMMON_SKILLS_NAME: 82 of 287
SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME: present on 278 rows but containing an empty array in every case

A more serious problem affects all of them. Across the full extract of 165,386 postings there are 2,025 distinct values in SKILLS_NAME, and not one begins with a letter between D and Z. The same holds for SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME, which carries 1,834 distinct values under the same constraint.
The practical consequence is that no posting in the dataset lists Python, SQL, R, Tableau, Power BI, Spark, or any other tool whose name falls in that range. The skill lists appear to have been alphabetically truncated before delivery.
We report skill findings from what is present and flag the truncation prominently wherever skills are discussed. This limitation affects the skill-gap analysis in Step 3 directly, and we have raised it with the instructor.


Remote and Onsite Indicators
REMOTE_TYPE_NAME classifies 142 of 287 postings. The remaining 145 are recorded as “Unknown”.
We verified that Unknown means unclassified rather than misclassified: every posting whose LOCATION text mentions remote work is already flagged Remote or Hybrid, so no records needed recovery. Unknown is reported as its own category and is not treated as onsite.

Location Fields
The location fields in the extract are unreliable. STATE_NAME holds a valid state name on only about 65 of 287 postings; the rest contain “United States”, “Remote”, city fragments such as “Francisco” and “Austin”, or blanks. The structured alternatives are sparser still, with STATE populated on 92 postings, COUNTY_NAME on 39, and MSA_NAME on 16.
LOCATION is the only location field populated on every row, but it is free text with no consistent structure.
We built a derived state column using a four-stage rule, implemented in scripts/clean_location.py:

Match a full state name inside LOCATION
Otherwise match a two-letter state code between delimiters
Otherwise fall back to the STATE column
Otherwise map a small set of bare city names to their states

Two-letter codes recovered at any stage are normalized to full state names so that “CA” and “California” do not appear as separate categories.


Postings with a recovered state: 205 of 287 (71%)
Distinct states represented:     29


The 82 remaining postings are genuinely locationless: their LOCATION reads “United States”, “Remote”, “US”, or “USA”. These are reported as Unspecified rather than dropped, since a nationwide or remote posting is a real category rather than missing data.


Industry and Occupation Fields
NAICS_2022_4_NAME is blank throughout the extract, so the industry label is taken from NAICS_2022_6_NAME, which reads “Computer Systems Design and Related Services” on all 287 rows.
For occupation we use ONET_NAME, a controlled vocabulary, in preference to raw job titles. Titles are free text, so “Senior Data Analyst” and “Data Analyst - Senior” would otherwise count as separate roles.
ONET misclassified eight postings, placing them under “Models”, “Actors”, or “Information Security Analysts”. Inspection confirmed all eight are genuine analytics roles, including Advanced Data Analyst, Business Intelligence Developer, and People Data Analyst. We kept them and grouped them as “Other”, since our title filter rather than ONET defines membership in the role family.

Inconsistent Labels
Employer names are not standardized. Three patterns appear:

The same company under different spellings, such as “Turnitin” and “Turnitinllc”, and “Anduril Industries” and “Andurilindustries”
Applicant tracking system URLs recorded as the employer, such as “Jobs.baesystems.com” and “Careers.pnc.com”
Job titles differing only in spacing, such as “Technical Consultant- Enterprise Data Engineer” and “Technical Consultant - Enterprise Data Engineer”

We left employer names as supplied rather than merging them, since any merge rule risks combining genuinely distinct entities. Employer counts should therefore be read as approximate, and the pattern is noted wherever employers are discussed.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Analytical Limitations
Five limitations carry into the rest of the project.
Skill lists are alphabetically truncated. No skill beginning with a letter from D to Z appears anywhere in the source extract. Python, SQL, R, Tableau, and similar tools cannot be observed. This constrains the skill-gap analysis in Step 3 more than any other issue on this page.
Experience requirements are absent. Both experience fields are blank across all 165,386 postings, so the analysis substitutes education where experience would otherwise be reported.
Salary reflects disclosing employers only. Pay appears on 39 percent of postings. Employers that disclose salary may differ systematically from those that do not, so salary figures describe the disclosing subset rather than the market.
The window is one quarter. The extract spans 2026-03-25 to 2026-06-29. Seasonal hiring patterns cannot be observed, and any trend over time within the panel should be treated as noise rather than signal.
The panel is a sample, not a census. 287 postings in one industry over one quarter is enough to describe patterns, not enough to estimate market size. Findings are stated as what these postings show rather than as claims about analytics hiring nationally.
